newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia's Taylor remarries, offers toast for peace.
newsitem.headline: Liberia's Taylor remarries, offers toast for peace.

text.p: Faction leader Charles Taylor, the man who launched Liberia's civil war back in 1989, remarried on Tuesday -- his 49th birthday -- and offered a toast for peace in his shattered nation.
Taylor, wearing a cream suit, married Jewel Howard, his partner of 15 years, in the tiny Saint John's United Methodist Church on a hill overlooking his Gbanga stronghold.
"Be faithful to each other and use this union as a symbol of national reconciliation and peace in Liberia," the officiating clergyman told them.

"We should toast not only for this wedding but toast for reconciliation in our country. Peace in Liberia and the end of violence," Taylor said later, raising his glass at the reception in the Central Agricultural Research Institute.
"No more should Liberia go to war."

Taylor's former wife Enid "Tupee" Sogbie, his eight children, Nigeria's foreign minister, Tom Ikimi, and General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led ECOMOG West African peacekeeping force, were among the guests.
The bride, deputy governor of Liberia's Central Bank, wore a white lace wedding gown and was attended by half a dozen bridesmaids, dressed in green and white.
She offered her new husband a birthday and a wedding day rendering of the song "I Swear" by American group All for One.
The couple have a son, Philip, aged 13.
Taylor's former wife has remarried to Liberian soccer star Jonathan Sogbie, who is based in Switzerland.
Taylor supporters said earlier the ceremony had been switched to Gbanga from the capital Monrovia for security reasons. Some spoke of a plot to kill Taylor on his wedding day.

The ceremony passed off peacefully and the only weapons in evidence were carried by West African peacekeepers who lined the seven miles (12 km) from the church to the reception but Taylor and his bride travelled in his bullet-proof Mercedes.
Liberia's civil war has killed well over 150,000 people in the West African nation, which was set up by freed American slaves in 1847.

Liberia's warlords agreed a peace deal in Nigeria's capital Abuja last August after a flare-up in the civil war in the capital and an orgy of associated looting killed hundreds of people in April and May.
Taylor, whose National Patriotic Front for Liberia is the biggest militia group and was in the thick of last year's fighting, says he will run for president in elections planned for May.
Under the peace deal, the factions must disarm and demobilise before elections.
The deadline for the end of disarmament, which all the faction leaders have pledged to achieve, is Friday.
West African leaders have threatened sanctions against anyone derailing the peace deal. Malu says that any fighters found with arms after Friday's deadline will be treated as criminals.
